title: Evidence-based analysis of online consumer information about prostate artery embolization for benign prostatic hyperplasia
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 50 Google-retrieved websites and 31 YouTube videos about prostate artery embolization (PAE). Reports shares of sources containing 'misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims' (28% of websites, 55% of videos) with explicit denominators, plus a strict 'inaccurate claims' sub-category. Numerator label is a composite that mixes falsity with evidence-strength/omission judgements, so the headline rows are coded QUALITY-borderline and the strict falsity sub-category is given as a CONTENT definition variant.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language Google/YouTube results; searches run by US-based authors, IP location acknowledged as a limitation)
estimates.date: Not explicitly stated; searches conducted circa late 2019 (online references accessed 18 Dec 2019; Google Trends 2004-2019)
estimates.measure_type: % of unique PAE-related websites containing misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims about PAE
estimates.denominator: 50 unique patient-oriented websites identified from 420 Google search results for 21 PAE-specific queries (first 20 results per query, 370 duplicates excluded)
estimates.definition: A source counted in the numerator if the evidence-based content analysis identified at least one claim about PAE that was misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based; non-exclusive categories were exaggerated claim (weak data), unsupported claim, inaccurate claim, minimizing or failing to disclose PAE risks, misrepresentation of data, and opinions or testimonials
estimates.misinfo_def: "assessing claims about PAE and other BPH procedures for validity and degree of supporting evidence"; sources with "misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims"
estimates.source_quote: Contains misinformation, inaccuracies, or non-evidence-based claims                        14                               28%
estimates.page_loc: p. 111, Table 3 'Sources containing misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims', Websites (Google) header row; same figure in prose p. 108 ('Misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims were identiﬁed in 14 sources (28%)') and in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two investigators independently analyzed and categorized all claims against the published evidence base and clinical guidelines (NICE/AUA/EAU), with a third study member as tiebreaker; no agreement statistic (kappa) reported
estimates.moderator_quote: All claims were analyzed and categorized independently by two investigators, with the opinion of a third study member serving as tiebreaker.
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY (not CONTENT) under the ambiguity tie-break: the composite numerator label can be earned by a source containing no false statement (categories 'minimizing or failing to disclose the risks of PAE' = omission, and 'exaggerated claim (based on weak data from retrospective or single-center experiences)' = evidence-strength). The paper itself calls this 'the prevalence of misinformative claims', so a CONTENT reading is defensible; an adjudicator wanting a CONTENT row should use the strict 'Inaccurate claims' variant row (4%) or 'Misrepresentation of data' (10, 20%). Rank-truncated first-20 search results -> denom_selection curated. QUOTE NOTE: the prose sentence carrying this value ('Misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims were identified in 14 sources (28%)') is split across the PDF's two columns in the plain-text extraction, so the contiguous Table 3 header row is quoted instead; the two agree exactly.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) DISCERN quality shares: '20 sites (40%) had DISCERN quality scores <3' and '22 videos (71%) had DISCERN scores <3', plus mean DISCERN 3.0 (websites) vs 2.0 (videos) - these are pure instrument-quality measures (QUALITY, excluded from prevalence) and would only duplicate the QUALITY reading already carried by the two composite rows. (2) '15 (26%) of the 57 general BPH-related websites' mentioned PAE - a topic-salience share, not a misinformation share. (3) Other Table 3 sub-categories, all /50 websites and /31 videos and non-exclusive with the rows above: Misrepresentation of data 10 (20%) / 8 (26%); Minimizing or failing to disclose risks 8 (16%) / 4 (13%); Exaggerated claims 5 (10%) / 1 (3%); Unsupported claims 3 (6%) / 0 (0%); Opinions or testimonials 1 (2%) / 9 (29%). 'Misrepresentation of data' (20% websites, 26% videos) is the next most defensible CONTENT variant if an adjudicator wants a broader falsity numerator than 'inaccurate claims'. (4) Sponsor subgroup shares: 6/16 (38%) of academic-institution websites and 8/15 (53%) of academic-institution videos contained misinformative claims - a source-type subgroup, not the paper's headline denominator, and it inherits the same composite-label ambiguity. (5) Risk/benefit mention shares (Table 2, e.g. 88% mention benefits, 58% mention risks) are completeness, not falsity. (6) Country left Global: the paper never states a search locale; the only geographic statement is a limitation that its IP address may have shaped result ordering.

rob.design: Cross-sectional search-engine content analysis, no human participants. Google and YouTube queried with 21 identical PAE-specific query strings in a cookie-free, cache-cleared, private-browsing session; first 20 results per query examined; 420 web results -> 50 unique websites (370 duplicates removed) and 420 video results -> 31 videos (371 duplicates, 15 clinician-targeted videos and 3 with <100 views removed; English-language only). Quality scored with the validated DISCERN instrument; claims judged for validity and supporting evidence independently by two investigators with a third as tiebreaker. No inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa/agreement %) is reported; the authors list subjectivity of claim classification as the first limitation. No search date is given.
rob.item6_quote: An evidence-based analysis of website content was performed, assessing claims about PAE and other BPH procedures for validity and degree of supporting evidence.
rob.item10_quote: Misinformative, inaccurate, or non-evidence-based claims were identiﬁed in 14 sources (28%).
